title: Rebating upkeep fees against holdings of other Prime Agents' tokens gives every Prime a standing incentive to hold its peers
content:
A.6.1.1.7.2.3.2.2.1.1 defines the rebate as applying "for tokens of other Prime Agents that they hold," and A.6.1.1.7.2.3.2.2.1.2.1.2 makes it concrete: "When paying Ecosystem Upkeep fees, Osero deducts the rebate from the fees it pays."

The implication the text does not spell out but plainly creates: holding another Prime's token reduces your own cost of belonging to the ecosystem. An Agent choosing between an outside asset and a peer Agent's token faces an extra, ecosystem-supplied return on the latter.

That is an alignment mechanism dressed as an accounting rule. Prime Agents that hold each other are exposed to each other's performance, so the harm from one Agent externalizing risk onto the ecosystem falls partly on Agents that would otherwise be indifferent. It manufactures mutual stake without requiring anyone to be altruistic.

The risks are the mirror image, and they are real. Cross-holding correlates Prime Agent balance sheets, so a shock to one propagates to the others that hold it — the ecosystem's diversification declines as the incentive works. It also creates circular value: Agents can hold each other's tokens partly because doing so is subsidized, which can support valuations that are not independently justified. Since the upkeep fee itself is assessed on market capitalization, the two mechanisms interact — the subsidy supports peer token prices, and peer token prices set peer upkeep obligations.
description: The rebate base is peer-Agent tokens, so cross-holding directly lowers what an Agent owes — converting a fee into a subsidy for mutual stake between Primes.
